content: 1. Decentralization and integration of healthcare services improve the connection between patients and treatment, as well as follow-up care. This approach also enhances community engagement by linking community-based interventions with healthcare facilities, optimizing access to services, encouraging care-seeking behavior, and improving retention in care. 2. In 2021, the World Health Organization (WHO) issued a conditional recommendation to initiate antiretroviral therapy (ART) outside of traditional healthcare facilities to reduce delays in starting treatment. 3. WHO recommends integrating hepatitis C virus (HCV) testing, care, and treatment into existing clinical services. These include tuberculosis (TB) services, HIV/ART clinics, maternal and child health services, non-communicable disease screening, sexual and reproductive health services (especially sexually transmitted infection clinics), mental health programs, harm reduction initiatives, migrant and refugee services, and prison healthcare systems. 4. The primary goal of integrating HCV services with other healthcare programs is to create a unified delivery system that facilitates access to hepatitis testing and treatment alongside other health services. 5. By making hepatitis B and C testing and treatment more accessible within healthcare facilities, the reach and uptake of viral hepatitis care can be expanded. This integration also allows individuals with HCV to address other health needs simultaneously, saving time and financial resources. 6. Achieving the global targets of 90% testing and 80% treatment coverage for HCV will require significant simplification of service delivery models. 7. Comprehensive national planning for HCV elimination should be based on local epidemiological data, existing healthcare infrastructure, current testing and treatment coverage, and available financial and human resources. 8. Simplified and standardized care algorithms should be implemented across the continuum of care, from testing to treatment and prevention. 9. Strategies to strengthen the linkage between testing, care, treatment, and prevention are essential for improving outcomes. 10. Decentralized testing and treatment services at primary healthcare facilities or harm reduction sites can promote better access to care. 11. Task-sharing models, supported by training and mentoring of healthcare workers and peer workers, can enhance service delivery. 12. Differentiated care strategies should assess patient needs at various levels of care, with specialist referrals for complex cases as necessary. 13. Community engagement and peer support are critical for promoting access to services, addressing stigma and discrimination, and ensuring continuity of care. 14. Efficient procurement and supply management of quality-assured, affordable medicines and diagnostics are necessary to support HCV care. 15. Evidence supports three key components of simplified HCV service delivery: decentralization of services from specialized centers, integration of HCV care with other services, and task-sharing with non-specialist healthcare workers. 16. Decentralized and integrated HCV services have shown higher uptake of HCV RNA testing and direct-acting antiviral (DAA) treatment among people who inject drugs and prisoners compared to partially decentralized or centralized models. 17. For the general population, decentralization and integration of HCV services into primary care settings have demonstrated high cure rates (sustained virologic response, SVR12) across all levels of decentralization. 18. Studies indicate that fully decentralized and integrated care models are associated with reduced stigma, improved access, and better outcomes, particularly for marginalized populations such as people who inject drugs and prisoners. 19. WHO recommends fully decentralized HCV testing and treatment at peripheral healthcare facilities and full integration into existing services, based on evidence of increased uptake and improved outcomes. 20. Expanding HCV services to primary and secondary care levels, harm reduction sites, prisons, and HIV clinics can increase access, reduce costs, and improve convenience for patients. 21. Integrated care models, such as one-stop-shop services, are particularly beneficial for people who inject drugs, who often face barriers to accessing healthcare and have high rates of loss to follow-up. 22. Surveys and studies highlight the importance of non-judgmental and non-stigmatizing approaches by healthcare providers, especially for people who inject drugs and those living with HIV. 23. Cost-effectiveness studies demonstrate that simplified, decentralized care models are less expensive and more efficient than traditional, centralized models, while achieving similar or better health outcomes. 24. Training healthcare workers to deliver client-friendly services and manage complex cases is essential for the success of decentralized and integrated care models. 25. The benefits of decentralization and integration, including improved access, reduced stigma, and better coordination of care, outweigh potential challenges such as the need for additional training and triage systems.
